concept_definition: How the participant emotionally responds, in their own account, to their shortcomings in following rules, meeting deadlines, or being punctual. Higher-scoring participants express genuine remorse, guilt, or shame about their slips, frame punctuality and reliability as matters of character or respect, and voice resolve to do better next time, even when they keep failing. concept_name: Enjoyment or pride in disciplined behavior
concept_definition: The affective stance the participant expresses toward their own rule-following, organization, punctuality, and deadline-meeting behavior: whether they convey enjoyment, enthusiasm, or pride in being disciplined, versus treating compliance as a neutral habit or purely a means to external outcomes (grades, advancement, avoiding trouble or harm), versus experiencing it as a burden, imposition, or dread-driven chore. This is distinct from rule-endorsement attitudes (opinions about rules in general), the anxiety-driver behind orderliness (worry or obsession), remorse over lapses (response to failures), and effortful engagement (whether striving occurs): two participants can both claim to meet every deadline, yet one conveys that they like and take pride in doing so ('i love it when people see me like that', 'I like to complete work well in advance', seeking recommendation for timeliness) while the other describes the same compliance as something tolerated to avoid trouble or to earn grades. interview_question: Describe how closely you follow rules and meet deadlines and provide examples
concept_name: Preserved versus sacrificed obligations under uneven compliance
concept_definition: When the participant's own account differentiates their reliability across domains (following some rules but not others, meeting work deadlines but not civic ones, being punctual in some settings but not others), the direction of the trade-off: which obligation type is preserved and which is let slip. Higher-scoring participants (roughly 4.5-5.4) keep deadlines, appointments, and commitments to others firmly met while relaxing peripheral rules (dress or convenience rules judged unnecessary, minor driving infractions, rules deemed unjust, or the letter of rules in favor of the spirit), or secure delivery by asking for help and turning down work they cannot finish on time. Mid-range participants (roughly 4.2-5.0) neither uniformly meet nor drop obligations but redesign them around their own manageability or alignment: setting self-imposed, more manageable deadlines with intermediate action items, or taking on only projects that fit their schedule, energy, or sense of meaning. Lower-scoring participants (roughly 2.35-3.95) show the reverse pattern: they preserve rule-following claims, ideological stances, or self-directed selection while deadlines and obligations deteriorate (forgetting tasks while claiming lifelong rule-following, meeting deadlines 'or get very close', filing taxes late when only principle is at stake, being exemplary only when financially rewarded, or declining others' deadlines in favor of own alignment without any delivery guarantee). This is distinct from deadline commitment bindingness (a normative stance about deadlines alone), deviation justification (reasoning about breaking a specific rule), and admitted follow-through lapses (whether failures occur): two participants can both admit uneven compliance, yet one sacrifices trivial rules to protect commitments while the other sacrifices commitments to protect rule-claims or self-direction, and this directional difference tracks the outcome.

interview_question: Describe how closely you follow rules and meet deadlines and provide examples
concept_name: Preserved versus sacrificed obligations under uneven compliance
concept_definition: When the participant's own account differentiates their reliability across domains (following some rules but not others, meeting work deadlines but not civic ones, being punctual in some settings but not others), the direction of the trade-off: which obligation type is preserved and which is let slip. Higher-scoring participants (roughly 4.5-5.4) keep deadlines, appointments, and commitments to others firmly met while relaxing peripheral rules (dress or convenience rules judged unnecessary, minor driving infractions, rules deemed unjust, or the letter of rules in favor of the spirit), or secure delivery by asking for help and turning down work they cannot finish on time. Mid-range participants (roughly 4.2-5.0) neither uniformly meet nor drop obligations but redesign them around their own manageability or alignment: setting self-imposed, more manageable deadlines with intermediate action items, or taking on only projects that fit their schedule, energy, or sense of meaning. Lower-scoring participants (roughly 2.35-3.95) show the reverse pattern: they preserve rule-following claims, ideological stances, or self-directed selection while deadlines and obligations deteriorate (forgetting tasks while claiming lifelong rule-following, meeting deadlines 'or get very close', filing taxes late when only principle is at stake, being exemplary only when financially rewarded, or declining others' deadlines in favor of own alignment without any delivery guarantee). This is distinct from deadline commitment bindingness (a normative stance about deadlines alone), deviation justification (reasoning about breaking a specific rule), and admitted follow-through lapses (whether failures occur): two participants can both admit uneven compliance, yet one sacrifices trivial rules to protect commitments while the other sacrifices commitments to protect rule-claims or self-direction, and this directional difference tracks the outcome.
